newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Nyerere asks world to give "Kabila a chance".
newsitem.headline: Nyerere asks world to give "Kabila a chance".

text.p: Former Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere on Monday said the world had to give victorious Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila a chance before it criticised him or set out blueprints for his future.
Nyerere, respected as an African elder statesman, briefed U.N. Security Council members after talking to the New York-based International Peace Academy.
He was particularly harsh on France for its actions in Zaire and Rwanda and refused to make Kabila responsible for reported massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire.
He also showed support for Rwanda's Tutsi government, and appeared to somewhat temper his usual tough criticism of Burundi's Tutsi leaders. He had attempted to negotiate peace in Burundi.
Nyerere, 75, said he had no idea what Kabila would do next.
"I don't know. I don't think he knows himself," he said, adding that no one was more surprised than Kabila at his quick march through the country.
"Please give Mr Kabila a chance ... to organise himself," he told the academy.

Nyerere said any talk of elections should wait at least a year because Kabila had not yet recruited a proper army, whose soldiers were initially supplied almost exclusively by Rwanda, or consolidated any kind of political base. Zaire, he said, had 150 political parties, many of them financed by Mobutu Sese Seko, the ousted president.
But Nyerere said he believed Kabila would recruit opposition figures for his government, even though "some of them are corrupt" but he should not be asked to include Mobutu's followers.

Zaire today, he said, was not South Africa where President Nelson Mandela and his predecessor F.W. de Klerk initially shared power. "Kabila is not Mandela and Mobutu was not de Klerk either. Mandela included everybody."
He scoffed at talk that the French era in Zaire was now over and the days of U.S. influence would begin.
"To us this in an insult. This is not 1885 but 1997," he said. "Why should a war between western Europe and the United States take place in Africa?"

And he said France took seriously the so-called English-French language war, which he contended made little difference to Africa. Rwanda's vice-president Major General Paul Kagame, for example, spoke English while the leader of Burundi, Major Pierre Boyoya, spoke French.
"So what? We had 700,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania. How many refugees were in France. If there were some, they were the rich ones," he said.

Nyerere said Kabila had been "demonized" by the Western media for the massacres of Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire when the situation was not of his making and many of the troops there were from Rwanda.

He said the West as well as the Africans did little to stop the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of Tutsis by militant Hutus before a million Hutus went to Zaire, the killers among them. "This is a new development, armed refugees," he said.
